sections.overview: The red kangaroo is a large grazing marsupial of mainland Australia’s arid and semi-arid interior. It uses open plains, grasslands and shrublands. Its fortunes follow irregular rain: fresh growth can support breeding and population increases, while prolonged drought reduces forage and may lower numbers.
sections.identification: The largest living marsupial, it shows striking sexual dimorphism. Males may reach 1.4 m head-and-body length and 92 kg; females about 1.1 m and 39 kg. Males are often rusty red and females blue-grey, though shades vary. Both have pale undersides and black-and-white cheek markings, including a light stripe from mouth towards ear. Fast travel uses powerful hindlimb bounds; a long muscular tail swings with the legs and helps reduce trunk pitch. During each bound, ankle extensor tendons stretch under load and recoil, returning stored elastic energy. This reduces the muscle work needed to repeat the movement; oxygen use on level ground changes little across hopping speeds, though uphill travel costs more.
sections.habitat: Across mainland Australia’s dry interior, it inhabits open plains, grassland, shrubland and savanna woodland. Scattered trees and shrubs offer shade from intense heat. In hot conditions, blood flow rises in superficial vessels of the forelegs; licking spreads moisture there, which evaporates and carries heat away. Radio-tracking in Western Australia found adult females’ core ranges stable and compact, with grazing and shelter together; males used larger areas. Drought increased adult dispersal, and journeys to water were prominent. Local distribution thus reflects vegetation and changing forage as well as water access.
sections.diet: It mainly grazes grasses. A 12-year study in southern Australian arid shrubland found more forbs in wet seasons and more shrub browsing in dry conditions; grasses still formed almost 90% of sampled food in severe drought. Microbes ferment fibrous plants in its enlarged forestomach, making nutrients available. Experiments with red kangaroos found methane yield varied with food intake. Green herbage supplies some water, but drought reduces both forage and moisture.
sections.behavior: Groups are small and temporary rather than fixed family units: one field study in northwestern New South Wales recorded a mean of 2.2 animals, with size and membership changing frequently. Radio-tracking found adult females relatively sedentary with stable ranges, while subadult males dispersed widely; drought increased adult movements. Male ranges were larger and could include the core areas of several females. In an arid-pasture study, grazing peaked between dusk and dawn, when animals spent over 60% of their time grazing.
sections.reproduction: Breeding can occur year-round, with more births in spring and summer, and responds to food and rainfall. After about 33 days, one very underdeveloped young crawls into the pouch and attaches to a teat. A female may mate again soon after birth. If the pouch young still suckles, the new embryo can pause at the blastocyst stage; this embryonic diapause delays development until the older joey permanently leaves the pouch. The joey exits permanently at about eight months but may continue suckling for months.
sections.ecology: The red kangaroo is prey for predators such as dingoes and shares arid rangelands with livestock. In a long-term southern Australian study, dietary overlap with sheep increased in drought, when both relied heavily on grasses; potential competition grew as pasture deteriorated. An analysis of 1978–2002 aerial counts across four South Australian areas modelled population growth against rainfall, harvest, kangaroo density and domestic herbivore density. The best model found a positive statistical association with livestock density, which the authors proposed could reflect resource availability beyond rainfall. These findings describe regional pastoral systems, not a universal effect of livestock.
sections.conservation: The Mammal Diversity Database reported the IUCN global category as Least Concern when consulted in October 2026, reflecting the species’ broad Australian range and large population. This status coexists with marked local fluctuations: drought can reduce forage and survival, while favourable rain can support population growth. Management figures are regional. A New South Wales government report dated 17 December 2025 set commercial quotas for 2026 and gave 2025 estimates for monitored zones; these guide harvest in that state rather than estimate the global population.
